title: Influence of fake news in Twitter during the 2016 US presidential election
screen_reason: Observational Twitter study (171 million candidate-keyword tweets, 1 June - 8 November 2016) reporting the share of the 30.7 million news-linking tweets that pointed to fake news and extremely biased news domains (25% combined; 10% fake news alone) and the corresponding share of users (12%). Quantitative shares with stated denominators.

estimates.measure_type: % of tweets containing a URL to a news outlet that pointed to a fake news or extremely biased news website
estimates.value_raw: 25% of these tweets spread either fake or extremely biased news (fake news 2,991,073 tweets pt=0.10; extreme bias right 3,969,639 pt=0.13; extreme bias left 609,503 pt=0.02, of 30.7 million)
estimates.denominator: 30.7 million tweets containing a URL directing to a classified news outlet website, sent by 2.3 million users, drawn from 171 million English tweets mentioning Clinton or Trump
estimates.definition: The URL's resolved hostname matched a domain in the fake news set (opensources.co 'Fake News' + 'Conspiracy Theory' categories) or the extremely biased set (opensources.co 'Extreme Bias', right or left)
estimates.misinfo_def: "'Fake News': sources that entirely fabricate information, disseminate deceptive content, or grossly distort actual news reports"; "'Conspiracy Theory': sources that are well-known promoters of kooky conspiracy theories"; "Extreme Bias" = "sources that come from a particular point of view and may rely on propaganda, decontextualized information, and opinions distorted as facts"
estimates.n: 30.7 million tweets with a news-outlet URL
estimates.source_quote:

estimates.page_loc: p. 3, Results, 'News spreading in Twitter'; also abstract and Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Curated domain list from www.opensources.co (media and communication research team headed by Melissa Zimdars, Merrimack College). Fake news set = 'Fake News' + 'Conspiracy Theory' hostnames; extremely biased set = 'Extreme Bias' hostnames not already in the fake set. Political bias of each extreme-bias site manually re-checked on allsides.com and mediabiasfactcheck.com; classification validated against Bakshy et al. domain-level alignment scores (R2 = 0.9). No inter-coder kappa. Authors state 'The classification of news as "fake" news or "extremely biased" news is a matter of opinion, rather than a statement of fact.'
estimates.moderator_quote: We collected tweets continuously using the Twitter Search API from 1 June 2016 to 8 November 2016. We gather a total of 171 million tweets in the English language, mentioning the two top candidates from the Republican Party (Donald J. Trump) and Democratic Party (Hillary Clinton) ... We discard insignificant outlets accumulating less than 1% of the total number of tweets in their category.
estimates.notes: Broad definition: numerator merges fake/conspiracy sites with 'extremely biased' (hyperpartisan) sites, so this is a source-reliability share and not a falsity share. Denominator is doubly restricted: (a) only tweets captured by the two candidate-name keyword queries, (b) only URLs to hostnames the authors classified (top-250 hostnames = 79% of all shared URLs, minus outlets with <1% of their category's tweets), hence denom_selection=curated. denom_scope coded topical rather than political_news because the corpus is a single-issue (2016 election) keyword harvest; an adjudicator may prefer political_news.

estimates.notes: ADJUDICATION FLAG. This is not a clean actor share of a fixed population. The Table 1 user counts sum to 4.27 million against only 2.3 million distinct news-sharing users, so the denominator behind the 12% is the sum of per-category distinct-user counts and double counts anyone who shared links from more than one category. The paper acknowledges this in the parenthesis quoted in moderator_quote. Denominator is also restricted to people who shared a news link at all, not to all Twitter users or all US adults. Keep only if the review accepts an overlapping-category denominator; otherwise drop.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) 'extremely biased news 15% of the tweets linking to a news outlet media' is verbatim but is the non-fake component of the 25% total, not an alternative whole definition, so it got no row (it is also a bias rather than a veracity category). 2) Table 1 gives per-category user proportions (fake news pu = 0.05, 204,899 users) but the pu column sums to 4.27 million against 2.3 million distinct users, so those denominators are overlapping-category sums and were not extracted. 3) pt,n/o = 0.19 (share of fake news tweets sent from non-official clients) and Nt,n/o/Nu,n/o = 80.35 (tweets per non-official-client fake news user) are automation indicators, not misinformation prevalence. 4) Retweet-network structure (Table 2), Collective Influence rankings (Table 3), and the Granger causal effects (Table 4) are not prevalence quantities. 5) No CONCENTRATION row: the paper reports top-100 influencer networks and states fake news diffusion 'seems to not be controlled by a small set of influencers', but never gives a top-X%-accounts-for-Y%-of-activity pair, so R1 cannot be satisfied. 6) '64% is in favor of Hillary Clinton while 28% is in favor of Donald Trump' is a partisanship split of the sample, not misinformation. 7) Of the 55 million tweets with any external URL, only 30.7 million linked to a classified news outlet; the paper never reports fake news as a share of all 55 million or of all 171 million tweets. QUOTE FORM: the text file is a -layout rendering of a multi-column print page, so the printed sentences are interleaved with the neighbouring columns and no full sentence is contiguous in the file; each source_quote is therefore the exact within-line column fragment carrying the value, and the full sentence is reproduced in value_raw / measure_type.

rob.design: Twitter Search API collection, 1 June - 8 November 2016, of 171 million English tweets mentioning Clinton or Trump (two candidate-name keyword queries), 11 million distinct users; 55 million contained an external URL and 30.7 million a URL to a classified news outlet, from 2.3 million users. Misinformation coded at the DOMAIN level (authors state article-level factuality is not assessed) using the third-party opensources.co curated list, with fake news = 'Fake News' + 'Conspiracy Theory' and extreme bias = 'Extreme Bias'; outlets with <1% of their category's tweets were discarded and only the top 250 hostnames (79% of all shared URLs) were classified. Bias labels manually re-verified on allsides.com and mediabiasfactcheck.com; external validation against Bakshy et al. alignment scores gave R2 = 0.9. No inter-coder reliability statistic. Bot handling by Twitter client string only (authors report high false-positive rate versus Botometer). Sample is not representative of Twitter or of the US public: 'our analysis focuses on news concerning the candidate of the presidential election published from the most popular news outlets and therefore its results cannot be directly generalized to the entire Twitter population'.
rob.item6_quote: The set of fake news website is constructed by joining the hostnames listed under the categories "Fake News" and "Conspiracy Theory" by www.opensources.co. ... "Fake News": sources that entirely fabricate information, disseminate deceptive content, or grossly distort actual news reports, "Conspiracy Theory": sources that are well-known promoters of kooky conspiracy theories.
rob.item10_quote: We find that, among the 30.7 million tweets containing an URL directing to a news outlet website, 10% point toward websites containing fake news or conspiracy theory and 15% point toward websites with extremely biased news.
